content: At the level of individual calls, the policy may involve reviewing every call record, a fixed proportion of calls (e.g., one in five), or only those calls involving poisonings of a specific severity. It is considered good practice to initially review all records created by new staff members. In poison centers where calls are electronically recorded and resources permit, a manager or senior staff member can listen to a selection of call recordings alongside the poisons information specialist. The handling of these calls can then be evaluated against clearly defined criteria, and any issues identified can be discussed. The assessment criteria may include the accuracy of the information recorded, whether an appropriate history was taken, the communication style of the poisons information specialist when speaking to the caller, and whether the correct information was provided. Routine auditing of calls in the presence of the poisons information specialist can highlight areas for improvement in call handling or identify the need for further training. The frequency and number of calls audited are determined by the poison center. Staff assessments every 3–6 months may suffice, provided that calls are also checked or peer-reviewed daily. Annex 8 provides an example of a call auditing form. Another component of quality assurance involves gathering feedback from service users to understand their requirements and expectations and to identify areas for improvement. Feedback can be collected by periodically sending a standardized questionnaire to a random sample of enquirers throughout the year. This questionnaire may take the form of an online survey, an emailed questionnaire, or a mailed questionnaire, depending on local circumstances. Each poison center should decide what percentage of their call volume to sample; for centers with high call volumes, a 5% sample may be sufficient. Suggested survey topics include the reason for contact, ease of access, quality of information provided, and staff attitude. Respondents are often asked to rate their satisfaction or dissatisfaction, and there should be a section for free-text comments at the end of the questionnaire, allowing users to provide any relevant feedback about the service. Annex 9 provides an example of a quality assurance form. The results should be compiled, reported, and used to implement any necessary improvements. The reputation of a poison center is heavily dependent on the quality of the services it provides. This, in turn, is largely determined by the competence, experience, and training of its staff. The center should also have mechanisms in place to monitor service quality, enabling prompt corrective actions when needed. Both training and quality assurance require resources, which should be factored into the planning of a poison center. Poison centers must have adequate and reliable funding to provide high-quality poisons information and maintain high standards for clinical and other services. Historically, poison centers were often funded by national governments, but many now rely on a combination of funding sources. A broad funding base offers greater financial security, protecting the center from funding shortfalls, although identifying and negotiating with multiple funding streams can require significant effort and administrative work. The operating costs of poison centers vary widely, influenced by factors such as the number and professional categories of staff employed, their salary scales, rental costs, database subscriptions, activities, and equipment maintenance and renewal costs. A clear understanding of these costs will help determine funding requirements and identify areas where costs can be reduced. Regardless of the funding source, there must be no conflict of interest for the poison center. Contracts or funding agreements must be justified and transparent, with clear statements protecting the center’s impartiality and independence. Failure to do so could lead to claims of bias, damaging the center’s credibility and reputation. Government health agency or department funding is a logical source for poison centers, as they play a critical role in improving clinical management and outcomes of poisonings, reducing healthcare costs, and protecting public health. They also contribute to toxicovigilance, enhance national capacity to address chemical threats, and help meet International Health Regulations (IHR) requirements. The value of these activities to the healthcare system and public health strongly supports the argument for government funding. Advantages of government funding include establishing the poison center as an integral part of the healthcare system, granting it authority and recognition, facilitating interactions within the healthcare system, and enabling collaboration with other government agencies. It also provides financial stability, allowing the center to plan strategically and focus resources on toxicological activities rather than securing funding. However, disadvantages include potential budget cuts if government priorities change, inflexible budgets, and strict conditions on how funding can be spent. Support from a host institution, such as a hospital or university, is often provided in kind, including physical infrastructure, access to facilities, and administrative support. Hosting a poison center can be mutually beneficial, enhancing the reputation of the host institution and enabling the poison center to contribute to research and training. In-kind support can significantly reduce administrative and financial overheads for the poison center. However, this support may depend on the financial position of the host institution, and internal charges may be introduced or increased if circumstances change. The host institution may also expect the poison center to adhere to its policies, which could compromise the center’s independence. Charging for certain clinical advice and services can generate income to fund poison center activities. Services that could be charged for include antidote provision, clinical toxicological consultations, poisons information advice, and toxicological analytical services. Charging models may include subscription fees, per-service fees, or internal cross-charging. However, charging for poisons information and advice may discourage inquiries, potentially delaying appropriate treatment and leading to poorer outcomes. It could also reduce call volumes, limiting toxicovigilance activities and data collection on poisoning epidemiology. To maintain financial stability and flexibility, poison centers should establish good business administration systems to manage contracts and differentiate between contracted and non-contracted users.
